# Build an app {#sec-app}

In @sec-website you asked for a web page and got one. That page *said* things. An app
*does* things: it reads your file, works something out, and shows you an answer. That is
where agents are at their most impressive, and where they fail most quietly. Ask for "a
page that looks up my genes in a DESeq2 table" and within a few minutes you'll have one
that loads, looks tidy and gives answers. Whether those answers are right is a separate
question, and the page won't tell you. A fold change read the wrong way round, an `NA`
treated as "not significant", `chr10` sorted before `chr2`: each one produces a page
that works perfectly and is wrong.

This morning's talk put the reason plainly. A one-line request leaves dozens of decisions
unmade, and the agent quietly **guesses every one**. Most guesses are reasonable. All of
them being right is the unlikely part. The fix is not a cleverer model or a longer
prompt. It's a **specification**: a short document that says what the app does, what it
doesn't, what goes in, and how you'll know it's right. It records the decisions, so
nobody has to guess them.

You won't write that spec yourself, and you won't write any code. The agent will
interview you, one question at a time, and write the spec from your answers. Then it
builds the app from the spec. Your job is the part only you can do: knowing what would
actually help in your work, and knowing the right answers for a small test case. This
chapter gives you a starter prompt that runs the whole conversation, from "what do you
work on?" to a working app in a folder on your laptop.

## What you'll learn

- What goes in a small, useful spec, and what goes wrong when each part is missing.
- Why a **test case with answers worked out by hand** is the most important part of it.
- How to let an agent interview you into a spec, rather than writing one.
- How to pick a way of building that needs nothing new on your computer, on Windows or
  macOS.
- How to read an agent's "what I checked" report, and what to do with "what I couldn't".

## What a spec is

A spec for a small app fits on two pages. It has seven parts (@tbl-app-spec-parts), and
each one exists because of a particular way things go wrong.

| Part | What it says | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Who it's for, and the one question it answers | The app grows features nobody asked for |
| **What it does** | A numbered list of behaviours | The agent decides, and each build decides differently |
| **What it doesn't** | Non-goals, said out loud | Plots, databases and logins arrive uninvited |
| **Inputs** | Formats, with a real example of each | It works on the agent's invented example, not your file |
| **Tiny test case** | An input small enough to check by eye, and its answers, **worked out by hand** | "It works" means "it runs" |
| **Open decisions** | Each choice, with a suggested default | Silent guesses, discovered months later |
| **Done when** | A checklist you can tick yourself | Nobody knows when to stop |

: The seven parts of a small spec, and what goes wrong without each. {#tbl-app-spec-parts}

The test case deserves a word of its own. An agent that writes the code *and* works out
the expected answers by running that code has only shown that the code agrees with
itself. The answers have to come from somewhere else: from rules written down before any
code existed, checked by a person. That's you. The rule that goes with it is simple:
**never change the answers to make a test pass.** If the code disagrees with an answer
you checked, the code is wrong.

::: {.column-margin}
**Fixture** is the programmer's word for a small test file with known answers. PeakPeek's
is 17 lines long, and every line is there to catch one particular mistake.
:::

The order matters as much as the parts. The conversation goes from your work to your
computer to the spec, and only then to code, with you approving the spec before anything
is built (@fig-app-loop).

## Worked example: PeakPeek

PeakPeek is a page that tells you what's in a peak file: how many peaks, how wide, on
which chromosomes, and what's wrong with the file. Its
[spec](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/blob/main/examples/peakpeek/SPEC.md)
is much longer than the one you'll write, about 440 lines, because it was written to be
built by a roomful of people without anyone to ask. But it has the same seven parts.
Its reference data are five public ENCODE peak files from mouse thymus
[@doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2493-4], with the right answers for each worked out with `awk`,
Python and `bedtools`, independently of any app. Its fixture is a 17-line BED file with
a blank line, a zero-width peak, a start that isn't a number, and a `chr10` placed to
catch anyone who sorts chromosome names as text.

With a spec that complete, **the building was not the slow part.** We gave a fresh agent
(Claude Opus 5.5) an empty folder, the spec and a single prompt, twice. It built the whole
page in 15 minutes the first time and 13 the second, and both pages worked first time,
with every test passing (@fig-app-peakpeek shows the finished version).

![PeakPeek, the finished version, with two ENCODE files loaded by URL: CTCF and
H3K4me3. The CTCF card's numbers (20,220 peaks, median width 344 bp, 6,003,019 bp after
merging overlaps) match the answers worked out with `bedtools`.](../images/app-peakpeek.png){#fig-app-peakpeek fig-alt="The PeakPeek web page. At the top, a drop zone and a box of two ENCODE URLs. Below, two cards side by side, one per file, each with tables of counts and widths, a list of problems, and bar charts of peak width and peaks per chromosome."}

What the builds got wrong is more instructive than what they got right. Almost every
problem traced back to the **spec**, not the code:

- **An undefined word.** The spec asked for a count of "overlapping peaks" but never said
  what counted as overlapping. Two builds chose differently and reported 1,763 and 3,457
  for the same CTCF file. Both were reasonable; they couldn't both be the answer.
- **A wrong definition, with the right answer.** The spec said the CTCF file had one
  "exact duplicate" line. It has two lines with the same position and different scores.
  The count of 1 was right; the description was wrong. A build found it.
- **A rule that contradicted itself.** "Accept `1e+03`, reject `1.5e2`" looks tidy until
  you notice that 1.5e2 is 150, a perfectly good whole number, and that R writes large
  numbers exactly this way.
- **Something that could never work.** The first draft had the test page read its
  answers from a separate file. A page opened by double-clicking isn't allowed to read
  other files, so that test could never have passed. The answers moved into a script.

**Every fresh build found something.** That's the case for running the check, and for
having a spec to fix: the correction goes into one place, and the next build gets it.
The finished PeakPeek is public at <https://github.com/seandavi/peakpeek>, and you can use
it at <https://seandavi.github.io/peakpeek/>.

## Worked example: the starter prompt, tested

The prompt you'll use in a moment was tested before it reached you. We played the part
of an attendee: a postdoc studying gene regulation in B cells, with a DESeq2
[@doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8] results table from the Vahedi lab's
[workshop data](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/tree/main/track-a/data)
and a project folder with the kind of `AGENTS.md` you wrote in @sec-teach. The agent was
Claude Code on a Mac. The answers were ours, typed from a script, so **your conversation
will go differently**; that's the point of it.

Here is what happened, stage by stage.

**The idea.** The agent read the project's README and `AGENTS.md`, then asked before
opening the data. Allowed to look at the first few lines, it checked the fold-change
direction against the raw counts itself (`Myc`: about 600 reads in the knockout, 1,600 in
wild type, log2 fold change +1.19, so positive means *lower* in the knockout, as
`AGENTS.md` said). It then offered three ideas, each built around a mistake the table
invites: a gene lookup that states the direction in words, a sanity report for any new
table from the core, and an exporter for significant-gene lists. We picked the lookup.

**Your computer.** Without installing anything, it reported the operating system and
versions of R, RStudio, Python, Node and git, then recommended a single web page, on the
grounds that it needs nothing new, works on Windows, and keeps the data on the laptop.

**The spec.** 130 lines, all seven parts. The test case was a seven-gene table: two
real genes copied from the file and five made-up ones, each built to test one trap: a
`padj` of `NA`, a symbol shared by two genes, a `padj` of exactly 0.05, an Ensembl ID
with a version suffix, and an ID that isn't in the table. It showed its working for each
answer and asked us to confirm them. It raised five open decisions, and flagged the one
that mattered most: keep the fold change as written in the file, and let the words carry
the direction.

**The build.** Two minutes. Its own test compared the page's output with our eight
approved rows and matched every one. It reported what it had checked, and what it hadn't:
it had not clicked through the page itself, nor tried pasting into slides. So we did:
the page, opened in Chrome and given the test file, produced exactly the eight rows
(@fig-app-gene-lookup).

![The gene lookup built in the test run, given its own seven-gene test table. Five of the
genes are made up, each to test one trap: a missing `padj`, a shared symbol, a `padj` of
exactly 0.05, an ID that isn't there. The yellow line states the direction of the fold
change at all times.](../images/app-gene-lookup.png){#fig-app-gene-lookup fig-alt="A web page titled Gene lookup. A yellow banner explains that log2FoldChange is wild type relative to the knockout. Below, a file picker, a box of pasted gene names, a Copy table button, and a table of eight rows with columns Query, Symbol, Gene_ID, baseMean, log2FC, padj, Verdict and Note."}

Three things went less well, and the prompt below was changed because of them:

- **Its test needed Node**, a programming tool many attendees won't have, especially on
  Windows. The prompt now asks for a test you can run with only what's on your computer:
  for a web page, a `test.html` you double-click. A second run of the revised prompt did
  exactly that, and its `test.html` showed 17 of 17 checks passing when we opened it.
- **It went beyond the spec without asking.** It added a second clipboard format so tables
  paste properly into slides. That was sensible, and it told us, but the prompt had said
  to ask first. The second run did the same with three small choices, listed them, and
  asked afterwards. Watch for this: an agent's idea of "obviously helpful" is still a
  decision, and decisions belong in the spec.
- **We rubber-stamped the answers.** Our script said "all correct" without checking. We
  checked afterwards, and they were, but that's luck, not a method. The second run's spec
  had eleven answers, including fold changes like 2^0.3^ = 1.23: easy to check with a
  calculator, and easy to skip.

In the second run, with the same scripted answers, the agent made a different and
arguably better choice: the app refuses to show results until you say which group a
positive fold change favours, because getting that backwards is the most likely mistake.
It asked before reading more than the first few lines of the real file, and the whole
conversation took under seven minutes of the agent's time, four of them building.
**Same prompt, same person, different app.** Neither is wrong. That's why the spec
exists: it's where you see the choice and make it yours.

## Your turn

You'll need about 30–45 minutes, most of it conversation. The build itself is usually the
short part.

### 1. Make a folder, start a new session

Make a new folder called `my-app` inside **Documents/agents-workshop**, next to the
folders from earlier chapters. Not inside your project from @sec-teach: the app is a new
thing, and it gets its own folder. Start a **new** session on it, as in
[Setup](00-setup.qmd) (in the Claude desktop app, choose the folder as the session's
project folder), and check with "what folder are you in?"

If you did @sec-teach, have the path to that project folder to hand. The agent will ask.

::: {.callout-important}
## Privacy: your data and the agent

The app itself can keep your data on your laptop: a page opened by double-clicking reads
files without sending them anywhere. **The conversation doesn't.** Anything the agent
reads, including "the first few lines of the data file", is sent to the model. The
morning's rule applies: nothing identifiable, no patient data, nothing unpublished you
aren't allowed to share. If in doubt, ask the agent to invent a small example in the
same format, and try your real file only in the finished app.
:::

### 2. Paste the starter prompt

```default
I'd like to build a small app with you: one I'd actually use in my work. I don't write
code, and I don't want to start now. Lead me through it in four stages, and don't start
the next stage until I say so. Ask me one question at a time. Look around before you ask
anything you could find out yourself.

Stage 1, the idea. Ask what I work on. If I point you to a project folder, read its
README and AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) first, and ask before opening anything else there.
Then suggest three small app ideas that would save me time or catch mistakes in my
work. Each should be something I could describe in two sentences and try on one file.
Help me pick one and cut it down to the smallest useful version.

Stage 2, my computer. Without installing anything, find out which operating system I'm
on and whether R, RStudio, Python, Node and git are installed. Tell me what you found.
Then pick the simplest way to build the app that needs nothing new. If in doubt, make
it a web page: one folder, opened by double-clicking index.html, with no server, no
packages and no internet needed to run it. It must work on Windows as well as macOS.

Stage 3, the spec. Write a short SPEC.md in this folder, two pages at most:
- Purpose: who it's for, and the question it answers.
- What it does, as a numbered list.
- What it doesn't do.
- Inputs: formats, with a real example of each.
- A tiny test case: an input small enough to check by eye, and its right answers,
  worked out by hand. Show me the working, and ask me to confirm each answer.
- Open decisions, each with a suggested default.
- Done when: a short checklist I can tick myself.
Then ask me to read it. Write no code until I say "approved".

Stage 4, the build. Build exactly what SPEC.md describes. Save the test case and its
answers as files, with a test I can run myself using only what's on my computer (for a
web page, a test.html I double-click). Never change the answers to make a test pass: if
the code disagrees, fix the code, or stop and tell me. If something needs more than the
spec says, ask me first. Then add an entry to LEDGER.md (start one if there isn't one),
with the headings Asked / Agent did / Checked how / Confidently wrong / Keep, and tell
me how to open the app, what you checked and how, and what you couldn't check.
```

### 3. Have the conversation

A few things make it go well.

- **Answer in your own words.** "I get DESeq2 tables from the core and I always forget
  which way the fold change goes" is a perfect answer. So is "I don't know, what would
  you suggest?"
- **Say "smaller".** The first idea is almost always too big. The smallest useful
  version is something you could try on one file this afternoon.
- **Take the suggested defaults** for the open decisions the first time through, unless
  one is plainly wrong for your work. You can change them later; that's what the spec is
  for.
- **Check the test answers yourself.** This is the one step you can't hand over. Work
  each one out from the rules in the spec, with a calculator if you need one. If you
  can't tell whether an answer is right, the rule is unclear: ask for it to be rewritten.
- **Read the spec before you say "approved".** Two pages. Anything you don't understand
  is a question worth asking now.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If it goes wrong

- **The agent wants to install something.** Say no, and ask for a way that needs nothing
  new. A web page almost always works.
- **The spec is long.** "Cut it to two pages; move anything optional to 'What it doesn't
  do'."
- **It stopped halfway through the build.** Say "continue".
- **A blank page.** Open the browser's console (⌥⌘J on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows,
  in Chrome or Edge) and paste the red text to the agent.
- **A test fails.** Ask "is the code wrong, or the expected answer?" You checked the
  answers, so it's the code, unless you find you made a mistake. If you did, fix the
  answer *in the spec* first, deliberately, and say why in the ledger.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## On Windows

- **Double-clicking `index.html`** opens it in your default browser, usually Edge. That's
  fine: Edge and Chrome behave the same here.
- **File extensions are hidden** by default, so `index.html` may show as `index`; see
  @sec-windows.
- **Checking what's installed**: the agent may run commands in PowerShell rather than a
  Unix shell, and ask permission for each. They only read version numbers; allowing them
  is safe.
- **R and RStudio** are often installed without being on the command line's path, so the
  agent may not find them at first. If you know they're there, tell it.
:::

### 4. Try it, then save it

Open the app and run its test first: every answer should match the ones you checked. Then
try it on a real file, and on something it should reject. Ask the agent about anything
that surprises you.

**@sec-project carries on with this app**, so keep the folder. When you're happy with it,
ask:

```default
Copy everything in this folder except snapshots/ into snapshots/first-build/.
```

::: {.callout-note}
## No idea, or no time?

Build PeakPeek instead. The spec is finished, and one prompt builds it:
[PeakPeek: a page built in one
prompt](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/blob/main/exercises/stretch-peakpeek.md).
Then come back and use the starter prompt on an idea of your own when one arrives.
:::

## What to notice

- **The questions found decisions you didn't know you were making.** Which way does the
  fold change go? Is exactly 0.05 significant? What happens to a gene that isn't there?
  Each one would have been a silent guess.
- **The build was fast; the checking was yours.** A few minutes of building sat behind a
  conversation several times as long. That's the right proportion.
- **"What I couldn't check" is the most useful part of the report.** In our test, the
  agent couldn't click through its own page. It said so. The page was right, but only
  because we went and looked.
- **Did it go beyond the spec?** Anything it added unasked is a decision somebody made
  without you. Put it in the spec, or take it out.

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-tip}
## You're done when

- [ ] Your folder has a `SPEC.md` you've read, with a test case whose answers you worked
      out yourself.
- [ ] The app opens by double-clicking, with nothing installed for it.
- [ ] Its test passes, and you ran it yourself.
- [ ] You tried it on a real file, and on one it should reject.
- [ ] `LEDGER.md` says what was built and how it was checked, including what wasn't.
- [ ] There's a snapshot in `snapshots/first-build/`.
:::

## Going further

- **A new session for the build.** For anything bigger than this, the Claude Code
  documentation recommends writing the spec in one session and building from it in a
  fresh one, which has nothing in its context but the spec
  [@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices]. The spec is the distillate; hand
  over the distillate, not the conversation.
- **Build it twice.** Give the same spec to two fresh sessions and compare the apps.
  Wherever they differ, the spec left something open.
- **A bigger spec.** [Spec first, then build: peak overlap](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/blob/main/exercises/stretch-spec-then-build.md)
  is a spec at the scale of a real project, and
  [peakwhere](https://github.com/seandavi/peakwhere) is that spec built by agents, with
  every decision and review on the record.
- **Keep going with your app.** @sec-project turns it into a project: a ledger entry for
  every change, a record of each decision, and a way back when a change goes wrong.
